calls.systemPrompt:
You write the summary at the end of a design interview inside Caret, a design tool. Every value is already decided and final.

- summary: 2 or 3 sentences to the user about how their foundation fits their product.
- rule: one sentence on how colour is used (for example, where the brand colour appears and where it never does).
- reasons: one sentence per topic on why that choice fits, grounded in what they said and chose.
- Write for someone who builds software but has no design vocabulary. Short sentences. Say what a choice does and how it will look. A design term is fine only next to its plain meaning.
- Never change, add or suggest a value. Never name a colour or font that is not in the list you are given.
calls.prompt:
Their product, in their words:
"""
Argus is an open-source monitoring tool for servers and applications, with an AI investigator built in. You run it on your own infrastructure with one Docker command, then add its SDK to your apps. It watches metrics, containers and processes, and when something looks wrong it investigates: it correlates metrics, logs and events and explains the likely root cause in plain language. Free and MIT licensed; your data never leaves your servers. The landing page should send people to the GitHub repo and the docs.
"""

The decided foundation:
- surface (light or dark): Dark
- display-type (the heading typeface): IBM Plex Sans. Shown with the reason: Drawn by IBM for engineers and dashboards, so headings sit naturally above metrics, containers and logs. It is open source like Argus, and stays clear even when a heading is small.
- body-type (the body typeface): Source Sans 3. Shown with the reason: Open shapes and a tall lowercase keep long log lines and metric labels readable at 14px on dark, and it looks clearly different from the IBM Plex Sans headings.
- type-scale (type size and weight): 16px body, headings ×1.25. Shown with the reason: Easy to read on a dark screen while scanning logs, and headings stand apart so the GitHub and docs steps are quick to find.
- brand-color (the brand colour): #28a4f0
- secondary-color (a supporting colour): #a78bfa. Shown with the reason: Sits next to your blue without clashing, and stays clear of the green, amber and red used for success, warning and error. Reads well on dark for chart lines and small buttons.
- accent-color (an accent colour): #f472b6. Shown with the reason: Pops against your blue brand and purple support, so a rare status dot or badge reads at a glance.
- neutral (the greys): Cool. Shown with the reason: Blue-leaning greys sit naturally beside your #28a4f0 and match the plain, technical feel of a server dashboard.
- semantics (success/warning/error colours): #22c55e, #f59e0b, #ef4444
- spacing (density and spacing): Tight, 4px base. Shown with the reason: More rows of metrics, containers and processes fit on one screen. Blocks sit close together, so the dark UI reads as a busy control panel. Good when you want a lot visible at once.
- radius (corner rounding): Soft, 8px. Shown with the reason: Lands on your 4px spacing base, so buttons, cards and panels feel like one tight system instead of mixed shapes.
- depth (shadows and depth): Subtle. Shown with the reason: Cards lift just enough to read as separate from the page while staying calm, matching your tight 4px spacing and 8px corners.

reply.summary: Argus is a dark, technical tool, so the foundation keeps everything tight and calm: a dark surface with soft 8px corners and subtle shadows that let many metric rows share one screen. IBM Plex Sans headings over Source Sans 3 body text keep log lines and labels readable, and your blue brand colour ties the page to the dashboard feel. It all points readers to the GitHub repo and the docs.
reply.rule: Your blue #28a4f0 marks links, buttons and the key headings that lead to the GitHub repo and docs; green, amber and red are reserved for success, warning and error, never used as decoration.

reasons.surface: Dark suits a monitoring tool you run on your own servers and watch at any hour, and it lets your blue #28a4f0, purple #a78bfa and pink #f472b6 stand out without glare.
reasons.display-type: IBM Plex Sans was drawn for engineers and dashboards, so headings sit naturally above metrics, containers and logs, and it is open source like Argus.
reasons.body-type: Source Sans 3 has open shapes and a tall lowercase, so long log lines and metric labels stay readable at 14px on dark and look clearly different from the headings.
reasons.type-scale: 16px body with headings at ×1.25 is easy to scan on a dark screen, and the clear size jump makes the GitHub and docs steps quick to find.
reasons.brand-color: #28a4f0 is the single blue that marks what you want people to click, so links to the GitHub repo and docs stand out against the cool grey background.
reasons.secondary-color: #a78bfa sits beside the blue without clashing and keeps clear of the green, amber and red used for status, so it works for chart lines and small buttons on dark.
reasons.accent-color: #f472b6 pops against the blue and purple, so a rare status dot or badge reads at a glance instead of blending in.
reasons.neutral: Cool, blue-leaning greys sit naturally beside #28a4f0 and match the plain, technical feel of a server dashboard.
reasons.semantics: Green #22c55e, amber #f59e0b and red #ef4444 are the standard, expected signals for healthy, warning and failing, so operators read them without thinking.
reasons.spacing: Tight 4px spacing fits more rows of metrics, containers and processes on one screen, so the dark UI reads as a busy control panel with a lot visible at once.
reasons.radius: Soft 8px corners land on the 4px spacing base, so buttons, cards and panels feel like one tight system instead of mixed shapes.
reasons.depth: Subtle shadows lift cards just enough to read as separate from the page while staying calm, matching the tight spacing and 8px corners.
